Can a power station run a home oxygen concentrator (5 L)?
Updated
October 10, 2026
SHORT ANSWER

Only as a short bridge. A 5 L home concentrator draws about 350 W nonstop, so a 1,000 Wh power station lasts about 2.5 hours and even a 4,000 Wh unit lasts only about 10.

Home oxygen concentrators are much hungrier than portable ones, at about 350 W for a 5 L unit. Inogen's At Home 5 L model uses a 275 W supply. Unlike a fridge, the compressor never cycles off. It runs the whole time the machine is on. Makers do not publish a start-up surge, so we plan for about 1,050 W, three times the running draw, which most stations can handle. The Jackery Explorer 300 v2, at 300 W of output, cannot run one at all, and the Goal Zero Yeti 500's 1,000 W surge is too tight to count on.

The battery is the problem. An 8-hour night at 350 W uses about 2,800 Wh, which needs roughly 3,300 Wh of battery after inverter losses. A full day uses about 8,400 Wh, or close to 10,000 Wh of battery. A 1,000 Wh unit lasts about 2.5 hours, a 2,000 Wh unit about 5 hours, and the 3,840 Wh Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus about 9.5 hours. Expandable systems can go further. With add-on batteries bringing it to 12,000 Wh, the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 would last about 29 hours.

That makes a portable power station the wrong tool to be your oxygen backup on its own. It can bridge a short outage or buy time until your supplier's backup arrives, and the units we list below are picked only for that job. A battery should never be the only backup for life-support equipment. Talk to your equipment supplier about what they provide for outages, and register with your utility's medical-needs program so they know your home depends on power. Use the flow setting your prescriber gave you, not a lower one to save battery.

Make it last longer
• Ask your equipment supplier what backup they provide that does not depend on electricity, and how quickly they can deliver it during an outage.
• Run the concentrator on its own. Every other device on the same station takes time away from your oxygen.
• Keep the station fully charged at all times, and recharge it whenever grid power, solar or a generator is available.
• If you also have a portable concentrator, ask your supplier whether it can cover outages. At about 40 W it draws far less, so the same battery lasts much longer.
• Keep the concentrator and the station in a ventilated room, away from curtains and bedding.

Common questions
How long will a power station run a home oxygen concentrator?
At about 350 W, a 1,000 Wh unit lasts about 2.5 hours, a 2,000 Wh unit about 5 hours, a 3,000 Wh unit about 7.5 hours, and a 4,000 Wh unit about 10 hours. Small 288 Wh units last about 40 minutes.
What size power station do I need for an oxygen concentrator overnight?
About 3,300 Wh of battery for 8 hours at 350 W. That means a 3,840 Wh or 4,096 Wh home-backup unit, or an expandable system. A 2,000 Wh unit covers only about 5 hours.
Can a small power station run a home oxygen concentrator?
Some can, but not for long. The 600 W EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus and BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 have enough output and surge, and last about 40 minutes. The Jackery Explorer 300 v2 (300 W) cannot run it at all, and the Goal Zero Yeti 500's 1,000 W surge is below the roughly 1,050 W start-up we plan for.
Is a power station a safe oxygen backup?
Not on its own. A battery should never be the only backup for life-support equipment. Talk to your equipment supplier about your outage plan and register with your utility's medical-needs program.

 Short answer

 Portable oxygen concentrators use less power than their chargers suggest. The Inogen One G5 power supply is rated up to 120 W, but Inogen's published draw runs from about 15 W at setting 1 to about 48 W at setting 5. Our 40 W figure sits near the top of that range. The unit pulls more, up to that 120 W rating, while it is also recharging its own battery.
 Surge is not an issue, and every station in our table can run one. Battery size is what matters, because oxygen is often needed around the clock. At 40 W, 24 hours uses about 960 Wh. After inverter losses, that is roughly 1,130 Wh of battery per day. A 288 Wh unit lasts about 6 hours, a 500 Wh unit about 11, a 1,000 Wh unit about 21 to 23 hours, and a 2,000 Wh unit about 43 hours. At 48 W, the top of Inogen's table, a 1,024 Wh unit lasts about 18 hours.
 Think of a power station as a bridge through an outage of a day or so, not as your main oxygen backup. Use the setting your prescriber gave you. Do not turn it down to make the battery last. A power station should never be the only backup for oxygen or any life-support equipment. Talk to your equipment supplier about what they provide for outages, and register with your utility's medical-needs program so they know you depend on power. For outages longer than a day, plan a way to recharge the station, such as solar panels or a car.

 Read this before anything else on this page
 A portable power station is consumer equipment, not medical equipment, and nothing here is medical advice. If you or someone in your household depends on supplemental oxygen, the three things that actually protect you are: the device manufacturer's own guidance on external power (it is in the manual, and some manufacturers name specific battery types), your equipment supplier, and your electric utility's medical-baseline or critical-care customer register, which in many states obliges the utility to give you advance notice of planned outages and priority restoration. A battery is a useful fourth layer. It is not a substitute for any of the first three. 
 With that said: the sizing question has a clear answer, and it depends entirely on which kind of concentrator you have. The two machines sold under that name differ by about a factor of ten in power draw, and almost every bad recommendation on this topic comes from treating them as one product. 
 Portable versus stationary: the whole decision
 Nameplate bands for the two concentrator classes. Read the plate or manual on your own machine — these are class ranges, not a figure for any specific device. Machine Typical draw Per hour Hours from 1,024Wh Hours from 2,048Wh

 Read the bottom two rows and the honest conclusion is plain: no portable power station in this site's registry runs a stationary home concentrator through a long outage on its own. A 1kWh unit buys you two to three hours. What a battery is genuinely good for is bridging a short cut, covering the gap while you move to a backup plan, or — with expansion batteries and solar input — stretching to something longer. Read the top three rows and the picture reverses entirely: a portable pulse-dose unit runs for a day or more from a mid-size battery, and for many hours from a 9 lb one. 
 The spec most buyers miss: switchover time
 If the point is riding through an outage rather than powering a trip, switchover is the specification to buy on, and it is not the same as capacity. In UPS or pass-through mode the unit sits between the wall and the device; when the grid drops, the inverter takes over. How long that takes decides whether the machine carries on or restarts. 
 Under 10 ms — EcoFlow publishes this for the DELTA 3 Plus. Fast enough that most mains equipment does not register the gap. 
 10 ms — Anker publishes this for the C1000 Gen 2 and the C300. 
 20 ms — EcoFlow publishes this for the DELTA 2 Max and BLUETTI for the AC180. Slower, and closer to the edge of what sensitive electronics tolerate. 
 Check the device manual for its own tolerance. This is the number that matters and only the device maker publishes it. Do not infer it from a power station's spec sheet. 
 Pass-through charging explained covers how that mode works and what it costs the battery, and power station as a UPS for wifi and router is the same setup applied to a simpler load if you want to see the pattern first. 
 Working out your own number
 Hours of runtime, from your machine's own plate
 Find the watts on the plate, or multiply the stated amps by 120 
 Usable battery = rated watt-hours x 0.85 (inverter losses and reserve) 
 Hours = usable battery / your machine's watts 
 Worked: a 400W home unit on 1,024Wh = (1,024 x 0.85) / 400 = 2.2 hours 
 Worked: a 35W portable on 288Wh = (288 x 0.85) / 35 = 7.0 hours 
 Worked: a 35W portable on 2,048Wh = (2,048 x 0.85) / 35 = 49.7 hours 
 The 0.85 factor is the part most online calculators leave out, and it is why real runtimes come in 15% under the arithmetic people do in their heads. Use it. 
 If the outage is the reason you are shopping
 Then size for a whole night or a whole day, not for the concentrator alone, and look seriously at expansion. Every pick above except the C300 has an expansion path or is already at 2kWh; best expandable power stations ranks the registry on exactly that specification, because buying a second battery later is far cheaper than buying a second power station. 
 Solar is the other half of a serious plan. A unit accepting 1,000W of input can put real watt-hours back during daylight, which against a portable concentrator's draw is more than it uses. How much solar input do you need has the realistic-harvest arithmetic, and best portable solar panels for power stations covers the panels. 
 And if the household need is bigger than a portable battery — a home concentrator plus a fridge for medication plus lights, for days — the honest answer is that you are shopping for home backup equipment rather than a portable unit. Best portable power stations for home backup covers where that line falls, and the 240V units at the top of it. 
 On the road
 For travel with a portable concentrator the constraints are different again: weight, recharge speed, and whether you can top up from a car. The C300 at 9.1 lb with an 80% recharge in 50 minutes is built for that, and the DELTA 2 Max's published 800W of car charging is the fastest route to refilling a big battery while driving. Charging a power station from your alternator explains how that works and where it goes wrong. 
 Flying is a separate matter entirely and the answer is restrictive: power stations are above the watt-hour limits airlines permit in either cabin or hold. Can you bring a power station on a plane sets out the rules, and concentrator batteries themselves are governed by different rules you should confirm with the airline directly.

 Can a power station run an oxygen concentrator? Runtimes from maker wattages
 Yes, but for far less time than most people expect. A typical 5-liter home concentrator draws 275–350 W by its maker's own spec, so a 1 kWh station such as the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 runs one for only about 2.5–3.1 hours. Treat a power station as a bridge that keeps oxygen flowing while you switch to the backup cylinders your supplier provides, not as your outage plan. Getting through an 8-hour night at 350 W takes about 3,435 Wh, which means a 4 kWh-class unit like the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3. The exception is a low-draw unit at a low prescribed setting: the Inogen At Home at setting 2 is about 100 W, and a 2 kWh station covers that for roughly 15 hours.
 Medical note. This page is general information about electricity, not medical advice. Your oxygen prescription, your doctor and your oxygen supplier decide your backup plan. Before an outage, ask your supplier for a backup supply that does not need electricity (cylinders) and learn how to switch to it, as the American Lung Association advises. Jackery says its power stations are not recommended for medical devices, and EcoFlow says its products are not intended for life-sustaining equipment. If you are short of breath or your oxygen is running out, call 911. Affiliate commissions have no bearing on any runtime or compatibility statement here; every figure comes from the device maker's published spec and the formula shown.
 How many watts a home oxygen concentrator draws
 A stationary concentrator runs a compressor all the time it is on, so it is one of the heaviest steady loads you can put on a portable power station and draws several times what a CPAP does. These are the makers' own figures for common 5-liter US models:

And most makers publish only an average or typical number, not the start-up surge of the compressor. The nameplate current is a useful ceiling: 3 A at 120 V is 360 VA for the Invacare and 3.3 A at 115 V is about 380 VA for the DeVilbiss. Every station on this page is rated for 1,500 W continuous or more, so steady output is not the problem; battery size is.
 The Inogen At Home manual also lists 275 W max; Inogen's 100 W figure is at setting 2. Philips lists lower figures for 220–230 V models; this page uses the 120 V numbers.
 Runtime by power station
 Hours on AC = Wh × 0.85 ÷ (concentrator W + 15 W inverter draw). Station Wh AC out Inogen At Home @2 (100 W) 275 W (275 W) DeVilbiss avg (310 W) Perfecto2 V (325 W) EverFlo (350 W)

 The 0.85 factor is our allowance for inverter and conversion losses, and the 15 W is the inverter's own draw (the figure BLUETTI publishes for its AC180); see the methodology . Real runtimes will be shorter in a cold room, on an older battery, or if the station also powers lights or a phone charger.  What it takes to get through a night

 At 300–350 W, 24 hours is roughly 9–10 kWh, the size of a home battery wall or several of the largest portable stations. That is why a battery alone is not a multi-day oxygen plan. Over a long outage, the options that scale are your supplier's cylinders, a generator running outdoors to recharge the station (see what size generator and generator vs power station ), or going somewhere with power. Solar helps but is slow: a 400 W panel array on a good winter day harvests well under one night's energy for a 350 W concentrator. Our 3-day outage planner shows the full budget for a household.
 Switchover and restart
 When the wall power drops, a concentrator stops and sounds its power-failure alarm. A power station in pass-through or UPS mode can keep it running without a gap, which matters because some units take time to come back to full purity: Invacare says the Perfecto2 V reaches its rated concentration after about 30 minutes of warm-up, and Inogen says under 5 minutes for the At Home.

 Test before you need it: with the concentrator running from the station and the station plugged into the wall, unplug the station and listen. No alarm and no restart means the switchover works for your unit. Also turn off any energy-saving or AC auto-off timer (Jackery ships the 1000 v2 with Energy Saving Mode on), and check that the station's fan noise and the concentrator's exhaust have room to breathe; Inogen asks for at least 6 inches of clearance and Invacare 12 inches.
 Portable oxygen concentrators (POCs)
 A POC is the easier load. It has its own battery (Inogen rates the One G5 at up to 6.5 hours on the single battery and 13 hours on the double, depending on setting) and can be charged from a power station. Two cautions from the Inogen One G5 manual :
 DC voltage. The G5's DC cable expects 13.5–15.0 V at up to 10 A. The 12 V car ports on the stations we track are listed at 12 V, below that range, so plan on the AC power supply in an AC outlet unless your station maker publishes a car-port voltage inside it.
 No published watts. Inogen lists the AC supply's input current (2.0–1.0 A), not average power. Measure your POC with a plug-in watt meter while it runs at your setting and charges a battery, then use the runtime formula above.
 Spare charged POC batteries and a car charger are on the American Lung Association's outage checklist; they cost less than a big station and don't depend on an inverter.
 A realistic outage plan
 Get a non-electric backup. Ask your oxygen supplier for cylinders sized to your prescription and how many hours each lasts. Learn to connect one before you need it.
 Register as power-dependent. Tell your electric utility, and local fire and police, that you rely on home oxygen; many utilities run a medical-priority program.
 Size the battery as a bridge. Pick a station that covers at least the time it takes to switch to cylinders or reach help, using the tables above with your unit's real draw.
 Plan the recharge. A generator outdoors, never in a garage or near a window, or a place with power. Carbon monoxide is a bigger risk than a dead battery.
 Don't turn the flow down to stretch the battery unless your doctor tells you to.
 Test twice a year: full charge, real unplug test, and a timed run so you know your actual hours.

 Questions
 How long will a power station run an oxygen concentrator? Divide the station's watt-hours by the concentrator's watts, after allowing for losses. We use Wh × 0.85 ÷ (concentrator watts + 15 W inverter draw). A 1,070 Wh Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 runs a 350 W Philips EverFlo about 2.5 hours and an Inogen At Home at setting 2 (about 100 W) about 7.9 hours. A 4,096 Wh EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 runs the same units about 9.5 and 30.3 hours.
 What size power station do I need for an oxygen concentrator overnight? For 8 hours, multiply (watts + 15) by 8 and divide by 0.85. That is about 3,435 Wh for a 350 W EverFlo, 3,200 Wh for a 325 W Invacare Perfecto2 V, 2,729 Wh for a concentrator at 275 W and 1,082 Wh for an Inogen At Home at setting 2. Use your own unit's spec at your prescribed flow, and add margin because batteries lose capacity in the cold and with age.
 Can I run an oxygen concentrator from a 1,000 Wh power station? Yes, for a few hours. Every 1 kWh-class station we list has enough continuous output (1,500 W or more), but at 275–350 W the battery is empty in about 2.5–3.1 hours. That is a useful bridge while you change over to cylinders or get to a place with power, not an overnight plan.
 Will a power station run a portable oxygen concentrator (POC)? Usually yes, through the POC's own AC power supply. Check the DC route first: the Inogen One G5 manual lists a DC input of 13.5–15.0 V, while the car ports on the stations we track are listed as 12 V. Use the maker's AC adapter in an AC outlet unless your station maker publishes a car-port voltage inside your POC's range. Inogen rates the G5 at up to 6.5 hours on a single battery and 13 hours on a double, depending on setting.
 Should I lower my oxygen flow to make the battery last longer? No, not without your doctor. The American Lung Association says not to reduce your oxygen flow rate to stretch a battery or oxygen supply without talking to your healthcare provider.
 Is a power station safe for medical equipment? Some makers say no. Jackery says its power stations are not recommended for medical devices, EcoFlow says its products are not intended for life-sustaining equipment, and Invacare describes the Perfecto2 V as not intended to sustain or support life. Ask your doctor and equipment supplier before you rely on any battery, and keep a non-electric backup oxygen supply.

results.text:
Backup Power for Medical Devices: How to Plan for CPAP, Oxygen and Other Equipment in an Outage - Preparing In The City 
 Skip to content 
 This post may contain affiliate links, full disclosure here. 
 Quick answer: if anyone in your home relies on a powered medical device, such as a CPAP, oxygen concentrator, nebulizer, powered wheelchair or home dialysis machine, make a written outage plan with your doctor and equipment supplier. Find each device’s wattage on its label, multiply by the hours you need to get watt-hours, and choose a backup with at least that capacity plus a safety margin, often a portable power station or the device’s own battery. Register with your utility’s medical program, keep a list of places with power, and know when to go to a hospital or shelter. Never run a generator indoors. 
 For most people, a power outage is an inconvenience. For people who depend on electricity to breathe, move, receive treatment or keep medicine cold, it can be a medical emergency. Planning ahead turns a frightening situation into a manageable one.
 This guide explains how to build a power plan for medical devices: who to talk to, how to estimate power needs, which backup options work, how to keep medications safe, and when to leave home. It is part of our emergency power guide to backup options for home outages .
 This article is general preparedness information, not medical advice. Always follow your doctor’s and device manufacturer’s instructions. Sources: Ready.gov guidance for people with disabilities and medical needs; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, HHS emPOWER Program; U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidance on insulin storage during emergencies; CDC guidance on carbon monoxide and generators; device manufacturer guidance on inverters and batteries. Checked October 2026. 
 Who Needs a Medical Power Plan
 You need a plan if anyone in your household uses electricity-dependent equipment, including:
 CPAP or BiPAP machines
 Oxygen concentrators
 Home ventilators
 Nebulizers and suction machines
 Powered wheelchairs and scooters
 Electric hospital beds and pressure-relief mattresses
 Home dialysis equipment
 Infusion pumps and feeding pumps
 Refrigerated medications, such as insulin
 The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services runs the HHS emPOWER Program, which uses Medicare data to help public health officials understand how many people in an area rely on electricity-dependent medical equipment. That shows how common this need is, but it does not replace your own plan.
 Step 1: Talk to Your Care Team
 Start with your doctor and your equipment supplier. Ask:
 How long can the person safely go without this device?
 Is there a non-electric backup, such as an oxygen cylinder or manual suction device?
 Does the device have an internal or external battery option, and how long does it last?
 What is the device’s power consumption?
 Is the device safe to use with a power station or inverter? What type?
 When should we go to a hospital during an outage?
 Ready.gov encourages people with medical needs to talk with their providers about how to prepare for power outages and to plan for backup power.
 Step 2: Find Out How Much Power You Need
 Read the label
 Every device lists its power use, usually in watts (W) or in volts and amps. If only volts and amps are listed, multiply them to estimate watts. For example, 120 volts times 1.5 amps is 180 watts. This is a maximum rating; actual use is often lower.
 Calculate watt-hours
 Watt-hours (Wh) tell you how much stored energy you need.
 Watts x hours of use = watt-hours 
 Device (example) Example power draw Hours needed Watt-hours 
 CPAP without humidifier 40 W 8 hours 320 Wh 
 CPAP with heated humidifier 100 W 8 hours 800 Wh 
 Nebulizer 80 W 1 hour 80 Wh 
 Medication mini-fridge 60 W average 24 hours 1,440 Wh 
 These numbers are examples only. Use your own devices’ ratings, or measure actual use with a plug-in watt meter.
 Add a safety margin
 Inverters and batteries lose some energy during conversion, and batteries should not be fully drained. Plan for at least 20 to 30 percent more capacity than your calculation.
 Our watt-hour worksheet for sizing backup power walks through the full calculation for a household.
 Humidifiers and heaters use more
 Heated humidifiers and heated tubing can greatly increase a CPAP’s power use. Many people turn off humidification during outages to stretch battery life. Ask your provider whether that is safe for you.
 For devices with humidifiers, such as many CPAP machines, running without the heated humidifier during an outage can greatly extend battery power. Ask your provider or equipment supplier whether that is safe for you and how to set it up.
 Step 3: Choose Backup Power Sources for Medical Devices
 Device batteries
 Many CPAP machines, portable oxygen concentrators and powered wheelchairs offer manufacturer batteries. These are designed for the device and are often the safest choice. Keep them charged and check their age.
 Many manufacturers sell external battery packs designed for their medical equipment. A dedicated battery backup from the manufacturer is usually the safest first option, because it is tested with your device.
 Portable power stations
 A portable power station is a large rechargeable battery with built-in outlets. It runs silently and safely indoors, making it a strong option for medical devices.
 Capacity: choose enough watt-hours for your needs plus a margin.
 Output: make sure the continuous wattage exceeds your device’s draw.
 Pure sine wave: many medical device makers recommend pure sine wave inverters, which produce cleaner power than modified sine wave inverters.
 Recharging: plan how you will recharge, using solar panels, a car or a generator outside.
 For a comparison of options, see portable power stations versus gas generators .
 Generators
 Generators can power devices for days, as long as you have fuel. They must be used safely.
 Run generators outdoors only, far from doors, windows and vents. The CDC warns that generators produce carbon monoxide, which can kill in minutes.
 Install battery-operated CO alarms inside your home.
 Use heavy-duty extension cords rated for the load.
 Consider an inverter generator for cleaner power to sensitive electronics.
 Read our full guide to generator safety, placement and fuel storage .
 Car power
 A car’s 12-volt outlet with an appropriate inverter or DC adapter can power some devices or recharge batteries. Run the car outdoors only, never in a garage, even with the door open.
 Non-electric backups
 Ask about non-electric alternatives, such as oxygen cylinders for people who use concentrators, or manual suction devices. These can bridge gaps when batteries run out.
 Some devices have a manual backup. For example, people who rely on suction or ventilation may be prescribed a manual suction device or a handheld resuscitation bag. Ask your provider whether a manual backup makes sense for your equipment, and practice using it before you need it.
 Device-Specific Tips
 CPAP and BiPAP
 Many CPAP makers sell batteries or DC power cords designed for their machines. Using a DC cord with a power station’s 12-volt output skips the inverter and can stretch runtime significantly. Ask your supplier which cord fits your model. Turning off the humidifier and heated tube during outages also saves power, if your provider agrees it is safe.
 Oxygen concentrators
 Home oxygen concentrators draw much more power than CPAP machines, which makes long battery backup expensive. Many people keep oxygen cylinders from their supplier as the main outage backup. Ask how many cylinders you should keep, how long each lasts at your prescribed flow rate and how to store them safely away from heat and flames. Portable oxygen concentrators with batteries can bridge shorter outages.
 Powered wheelchairs and scooters
 Keep chairs fully charged, especially when storms are forecast. Know your chair’s range on a full charge. If power will be out for a long time, find a place where you can recharge, such as a library, community center or friend’s home.
 Keep motorized wheelchairs and scooters fully charged whenever a storm is forecast, and know where you could recharge if the power is out for days. A manual wheelchair as a backup can keep you mobile if the battery runs down.
 Electric beds and pressure mattresses
 Most electric beds can be locked in a safe position without power. Pressure-relief air mattresses may deflate, so ask your provider about a backup mattress or how long the mattress will hold pressure.
 Home dialysis
 Home dialysis patients should have a specific emergency plan from their dialysis center, including an emergency diet, backup supplies and a list of alternative dialysis locations.
 Practice Your Backup Power Plan for Medical Devices
 Run a test during the day: unplug the device, switch to backup power and time how long it runs. Practicing helps everyone in the home learn the steps, reveals problems while there is still time to fix them and builds confidence for a real outage at night.
 Step 4: Register With Your Utility and Local Agencies
 Utility medical programs
 Many utilities let customers who rely on medical equipment register for medical certificate or medical baseline programs. Registration may provide advance notice of planned outages, protection from shutoffs for nonpayment or bill discounts. It generally does not guarantee faster restoration during widespread outages, so you still need a backup plan.
 Local emergency registries
 Some cities and counties keep voluntary registries of residents with medical needs to help plan emergency responses. Ask your local emergency management office.
 Tell your supplier and neighbors
 Let your equipment supplier know your plan, and ask whether they offer emergency delivery of oxygen or batteries. Share your plan with a trusted neighbor or family member who can check on you.
 Step 5: Keep Refrigerated Medicines Safe
 Some medicines need refrigeration. During an outage:
 Keep the refrigerator closed as much as possible.
 Use a cooler with ice packs for medicines if the outage lasts long. Avoid letting medicine freeze or touch ice directly.
 Check storage guidance: the FDA notes that insulin can generally be kept unrefrigerated at temperatures between 59 and 86 degrees Fahrenheit for up to 28 days, depending on the product. Check your medicine’s label.
 Ask your pharmacist about other medicines and replace any that may have been damaged.
 Our guide to food safety in a power outage explains how long refrigerators and freezers stay cold.
 Step 6: Know When to Leave
 Even a good plan has limits. Decide in advance when you will go elsewhere.
 When batteries are expected to run out before power is restored
 When heat or cold becomes dangerous
 When the person’s condition worsens
 When officials issue evacuation orders
 Possible destinations include a hospital, a friend’s or relative’s home with power, a hotel or a public shelter. Call ahead if possible. Some areas offer special needs shelters with power for medical equipment; check with your local emergency management office before an emergency.
 Special Considerations for Apartments
 In apartments and high-rises, elevators stop during outages, which can trap people who use wheelchairs or have mobility limits. Plan for evacuation help, keep backup power on hand and tell building management about your needs. Our guide to preparing for a power outage in a high-rise covers more.
 Build a Medical Device Emergency Kit
 Keep a dedicated emergency kit next to your medical equipment so everything is in one place:
 Charged battery packs and chargers, including a car charger if your device supports one
 Device manuals and the supplier’s 24-hour phone number
 A written list of devices, settings and power needs (watts and watt-hours)
 Spare supplies such as tubing, filters, masks and cannulas
 Any manual backup your provider recommends
 A flashlight or headlamp and a copy of your medication list
 Community resources
 During long outages, some communities open charging stations, cooling or warming centers, or shelters that can support medical equipment. Your local emergency management office, utility or 211 can tell you what is available, and some areas offer transport help for people who depend on electricity for health.
 Medical Power Plan Checklist
 List all electricity-dependent devices and medicines.
 Record each device’s wattage and battery runtime.
 Calculate watt-hours needed for at least 24 to 72 hours.
 Buy and test backup batteries or a power station.
 Keep batteries charged and check them monthly.
 Register with your utility’s medical program.
 Keep a printed list of your devices, settings, doctors and supplier numbers.
 Identify places to go if power will be out for a long time.
 Install CO alarms if you use a generator.
 Review the plan every six months.
 Keeping Battery Backup for Medical Devices Ready
 Batteries lose capacity over time and in storage.
 Charge power stations every few months, following manufacturer instructions.
 Test runtime by running your device on battery before an emergency.
 Replace batteries that no longer hold enough charge.
 Store batteries at moderate temperatures.
 Getting Help Paying for Backup Power
 Backup power can be expensive. Ask your doctor about a letter of medical necessity, check whether your insurer or Medicaid program covers device batteries, and ask local disability organizations, utilities or emergency management offices whether they offer assistance programs.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 How long will a power station run my CPAP?
 Divide the power station’s usable watt-hours by your CPAP’s wattage. For example, a 500 Wh station running a 40-watt CPAP without humidification might last around 10 hours after accounting for conversion losses. Test your own setup.
 Can I run medical equipment on a generator?
 Many devices can run on generator power, but generators must be used outdoors only. An inverter generator provides cleaner power for sensitive electronics.
 Will my utility restore my power first if I register?
 Not necessarily. Medical registration may provide notifications or other protections, but it usually does not guarantee priority restoration during widespread outages.
 What should I do if my oxygen concentrator loses power?
 Switch to your backup oxygen supply or battery as directed by your provider. If you have no backup or your condition worsens, seek medical help.
 How should I store insulin during a power outage?
 Follow the label. The FDA notes that many insulins can be kept unrefrigerated between 59 and 86 degrees Fahrenheit for up to 28 days.
 Should I turn off my CPAP humidifier during a power outage?
 Many CPAP users can extend battery runtime a lot by turning off the heated humidifier. Check with your provider or supplier first to confirm it is safe for your therapy.
 What is a manual backup for medical equipment?
 A manual backup is a device that works without power, such as a manual suction device or handheld resuscitation bag. Ask your provider whether you need one and how to use it.
 Sources

 HHS ASPR: HHS emPOWER Program.

 This guide is for people who need a concentrator to keep running when the grid does not. That is a harder job than a CPAP or a phone, because a concentrator draws its load continuously for as long as it is switched on, and because the battery gets charged every single day rather than a few times a year. We compared four units on the four specifications that decide the outcome: continuous inverter output, rated capacity, rated cycle life and solar input ceiling. We did not test any of them with a concentrator, and every review states exactly what its recommendation rests on. What you get here is the hours arithmetic at three stated machine loads, cycle ratings converted into years of nightly charging, and an honest look at which solar ceilings actually refill a pack rather than just slowing it down.
 What is the best portable power station for an oxygen concentrator?
 The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 suits the most households. Its 2600W continuous inverter is the largest here, so a stationary concentrator's compressor start is never in doubt, and its rating of over 6,000 cycles is about 16 years of charging it every night. If your outages run past a single night, the Anker SOLIX F3800 is the only unit here that runs a stationary machine for close to ten hours on one charge, roughly twice what the 2kWh units manage.
 Key takeaways
 Continuous inverter rating decides whether a compressor starts; capacity only decides how many hours follow
 Cycle life is the specification oxygen households should read first, because they cycle the pack nightly rather than seasonally
 A solar ceiling below your machine's draw never refills the battery, it only makes the drain slower
 Boost modes such as X-Boost and Power Lifting reach their headline wattage by lowering voltage, so they do nothing for a compressor

 What to look for before you buy
 Start with the plate on the machine, not the battery # 
 Almost every bad purchase here starts with watt-hours. The first question is not
how big the pack is. It is whether the inverter can start what you are plugging
into it, and then what the machine draws once it settles.
 A stationary concentrator runs a compressor. Compressors pull several times their
running draw for a fraction of a second at start-up, and that spike is what trips
an undersized inverter. When it trips, the machine stops, which is the one outcome
you bought the battery to prevent.
 A concentrator is also a continuous duty load, and that phrase matters when you
read an inverter’s specification sheet. Continuous duty means the machine holds
its draw for hours without pause, so the number to compare against it is the
inverter’s continuous rating, not any peak or surge figure. Some inverters are
rated to sustain their headline output only for a short window before they step
down or shut off. A concentrator will find that limit on the first night.
 That is why the continuous rating is the first number in every review here, and
why the boost figures printed beside it are not.
 The three loads this guide is built on # 
 Concentrators vary enormously, so we work from three stated assumptions and tell
you to replace them with your own machine’s figure:
 A pulse-dose portable, roughly 60W on average
 A continuous-flow portable, roughly 130W
 A stationary 5 LPM machine, roughly 350W
 We also assume 90% of a pack’s rated watt-hours actually reach the socket. Some of
every battery goes to inverter conversion and the unit’s own electronics, and no
manufacturer runtime chart accounts for it.
 The hours each unit holds # 
 Applying that to the rated capacities:
 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2, 2073.6Wh: about 5.3 hours at 350W, 14.4 at 130W, 31 at 60W
 Anker SOLIX S2000, 2010Wh: about 5.2 hours at 350W, 13.9 at 130W, 30 at 60W

 The pattern is worth sitting with. Three of these four units sit within 64Wh of
each other and land inside ten minutes of each other on a stationary machine. On
that load, capacity is not what distinguishes them. Everything else on this page
is.
 Cycle life is the specification nobody reads # 
 A camper charges a power station perhaps twenty times a year. An oxygen household
charges it every night. Divide each rated cycle count by 365 and the difference
becomes obvious:
 Anker SOLIX S2000, 10,000 cycles: about 27 years
 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2, over 6,000 cycles: about 16 years
 EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max, 3,000 cycles to 80%: about 8 years

 None of those are bad batteries. But if the unit is going to work every night
rather than sit on standby, the gap between eight years and twenty-seven is the
difference between buying once and buying twice.
 Getting past the first battery # 
 Five hours covers a normal outage. It does not cover a storm.
 There are two ways past it and both are worth understanding before you choose.
The first is recharge speed, which decides how much of a brief grid window you can
capture. The F3800 returns roughly 2,560Wh per hour of mains, the Elite 200 V2
about 1,659Wh on Turbo, the DELTA 2 Max about 1,489Wh.
 The second is solar, and here the trap is assuming panels deliver their rating.
Plan at roughly 60% and check the number against your machine’s draw. A 400W
ceiling becomes about 240W, which is below a 350W stationary machine, so the pack
still empties while the sun is up. A 1000W ceiling becomes about 600W and banks
250W an hour on top of running the machine. A 2400W ceiling banks over a kilowatt.
 If your machine draws more than your panels realistically make, solar is a
delaying tactic, not a solution.
 Where the ceiling really is # 
 Expansion is the only route to genuine multi-day coverage. The DELTA 2 Max grows
from 2kWh to 6kWh, which is about 15 hours on a stationary machine. The F3800
grows to 26.9kWh, which is roughly 69 hours, or close to three days.
 Everything below that is measured in hours, and should be planned in hours.
 What a battery does not replace # 
 None of this is medical advice. Say the important part plainly: a battery is not
a substitute for prescribed emergency oxygen. A power station only keeps a
working machine running for a known number of hours. It supplies electricity, not
oxygen, and it does nothing at all if the machine itself fails.
 So the cylinder backup your equipment provider arranges stays part of the plan,
and the power station sits in front of it. Register your address with the utility
as a medical priority too, so restoration crews know you are there.
 Buy the battery for the hours it genuinely gives you, and size the rest of the
plan around what happens after those hours run out.

 Questions buyers ask
 Is it safe to run an oxygen concentrator from a battery indoors?
 A battery power station burns no fuel and produces no exhaust, so unlike a petrol generator it carries no carbon monoxide risk indoors. Keep the vents clear and give it air, because these units run cooling fans under load and while charging, and never run a fuel generator inside for this job.
 Does an oxygen concentrator need a pure sine wave inverter?
 Yes, treat it as a requirement. A concentrator runs a compressor motor and a control board, and a modified sine wave supply can make motors run hot and confuse electronics. All four units here output pure sine wave AC, which is why the question rarely comes up in this class.
 How do I know what my own machine draws?
 Read the plate on the back or the base of the unit, or the power section of its manual. It will give either a wattage or an amperage. If it gives amps, multiply by 120 for a US supply to get watts. Use that number in place of our assumptions, because machines vary widely by flow rate and model.
 Will one of these hold enough charge if I leave it plugged in for months?
 Left on mains as a pass-through, all four sit at or near full and top themselves up, so they are ready when the grid drops. What that costs you is cycles and calendar age on the cells, which is why the rated cycle count in each review is worth reading before you decide to leave one permanently online.
 What happens when the battery runs out and the power is still off?
 That is the scenario to plan for before you buy, not during. A power station buys hours, and the arithmetic in this guide tells you roughly how many. It is a layer in front of the emergency supply your equipment provider arranges, not a replacement for it. Talk to that provider about cylinder backup and about registering your address with the utility as a medical priority.
